title: Before you start
note: One pretest for everyone since 2026-11-13: two screening questions (q1, q2: a course on bandits or reinforcement learning, or being able to explain an algorithm such as UCB, flag the session excluded), then five knowledge items, each with "I don't know" and no written reason, in one set (`final`): k1 (interval width and √n) and k2 (logarithmic growth), the maths the lesson builds on; h3 (few against many reviews), h4 (choosing on few results) and r3b (you only learn about what you choose), everyday statistical reasoning behind the post-test, with no algorithm named. Chosen from the team's sets C1 (k1, k2, r1, r2, r3) and C2 (h1 to h5, their twins), which the pilot took both: the pilots couldn't rank the items (one newcomer answered them all), so the choice rests on wording, cues and time: k1 and k2 need less arithmetic than h1 and h2; r1 is Wainer's textbook example of small schools; r2's key was the cautious middle option and r3's the only “No” among three “Yes” options. h4 is reworded and r3b is new (2026-11-13). Everything taken out is in stash/pretest.json. About 5 minutes (Oskar's times). It checks that the groups start alike and gives a covariate; with the test it gives pre and post percentages, which measure different things (prerequisites against the rules).

items.prompt: Have you taken a course on reinforcement learning, or covered multi-armed bandits in any course?
Before today, how well did you know multi-armed bandits?
options: I had never heard of them
I knew roughly how they work
I could explain an algorithm such as UCB
items.note: The team's proposal: (c) is recorded, (d) is excluded.

items.prompt: You estimate the true average of a noisy measurement twice, once from 10 readings and once from 1,000 readings. Compared with the 95% confidence interval from 1,000 readings, how wide is the interval from 10 readings?
diagnosis: the width does not depend on the number of readings
width proportional to the number of readings
items.explain: The width shrinks with √n, and √(1,000 / 10) = 10. With only 10 readings the t-value makes it about 11 times, still closest to (c). It underlies why the bonus of a rarely tried option is large and shrinks with every try (F10).

items.prompt: A quantity equals ln(t). As t goes from 10 to 100, it rises by about 2.3. How much further must t grow for the quantity to rise by another 2.3?
diagnosis: logarithm confused with a curve that levels off
equal steps in t give equal rises
the needed step doubles each time
items.explain: ln(1,000) − ln(100) = ln(10) ≈ 2.3, so each equal rise needs t to grow tenfold. It underlies why an unpicked option's bonus keeps growing without limit but takes ever longer to grow by the same amount (F11; V4, T9).

items.measures: few against many reviews, both ends
items.prompt: Restaurant A has an average of 4.8 stars from 5 reviews; restaurant B has 4.6 stars from 500 reviews. Which restaurant's true average is more likely to be above 4.9, and which is more likely to be below 4.5?
diagnosis: the lower average looks more likely to be too low
more reviews, more room for extreme values
items.explain: With 5 reviews, A's true average can lie far from 4.8 in either direction; with 500 reviews, B's lies very close to 4.6.
items.note: The key held in a Bayesian simulation under three different assumptions about typical ratings.

items.prompt: Shops X and Y each try out the same 20 suppliers, then give a big order to the one that did best. X tried each supplier once, Y ten times. Whose big order will likely fall further below how its supplier did in the trial?
options: Neither: both will match the trial
diagnosis: more test deliveries give more chances for a lucky high score
both picked their best supplier, so both are equally lucky
the best test results show the true quality
items.explain: Picking the best of 20 single deliveries mostly picks luck, while averages of ten deliveries contain much less of it. It underlies why greedy's choice after one try per option is unreliable.
items.note: In simulation (20 suppliers, true quality 70 ± 5, each delivery ± 10), X's chosen supplier fell short by 17 points on average and Y's by 3. Reworded 2026-11-13 (Phil: the setup read as complicated): shops instead of companies, "did best" instead of "the best test results"; the same options and key.

items.measures: you only learn about what you choose
items.prompt: A bank lends only to applicants its scoring rule rates as safe, and records whether each loan is repaid. So far 97% have been repaid. Does the rule turn away many people who would have repaid? What do the bank's records show?
options: That it turns away few of them
That it turns away many of them
Nothing, however many loans it records
Nothing yet; more years of records will show it
diagnosis: a high repayment rate among those accepted shows the rule rarely errs
a very high repayment rate shows the rule is too cautious
items.explain: The records hold only the applicants the rule accepted: someone turned away never gets a loan, so never produces a repayment record. The rate among the accepted says nothing about the rejected, and more years of the same records don't either. In bandit terms, an option that is never chosen never produces data (F2, F5).
items.note: New 2026-11-13, in place of r3 (Phil: too easy; its key was the only “No” among three “Yes” options, and the question nearly gave it away). Two readings of the 97% (few, many) and two answers on whether more records help; no option gives a reason, and the key isn't the longest.
